extracted.subtask_description: A multi-topic Associated Press news article from May 1943 reporting on wartime events, Supreme Court decisions, government actions, and public statistics. It is written for a general news audience and covers legal rulings, military actions, and domestic economic data in a single dispatch-style piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communications Commission authority under the Communications Act of 1934
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The communications act of 1934 authorized the commission to promulgate regulations designed to correct the abuses disclosed by its investigation of chain broadcasting.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court (Justice Frankfurter) treats the statute as granting regulatory power to the FCC to address abuses revealed by investigation; the existence of statutory authorization supports upholding the Commission’s regulations if based on such findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial-review standard for agency action
rubrics_metrics.description: “Our duty … is at an end when we find that the action of the commission was based upon findings supported by evidence, and was made to [within the authority granted by Congress].”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court will not decide the desirability of agency regulations; its review focuses on whether the agency’s action is supported by evidence and within statutory authority. Questions of public policy or desirability are left to Congress and the agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing standard: ‘public convenience or necessity’
rubrics_metrics.description: “The licensing system established by Congress in the communications act of 1934 … provided for the licensing of [stations] on ‘convenience or necessity.’ Denial of a station license on that ground is not a denial of free speech.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensing decisions grounded on the statutory standard of ‘public convenience or necessity’ are constitutionally permissible and do not equate to impermissible suppression of free speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for clear congressional mandate before regulating contractual relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice Murphy’s dissent: the 1934 communications act ‘does not in terms give the commission power to regulate the contractual relations between the stations and the networks,’ and the commission is not justified in exercising assumed authority 'without a clear mandate from the Congress.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a regulation reaches contractual relations not explicitly authorized by statute, at least some justices require a clear congressional grant of power before an agency may lawfully regulate those matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance of chain-broadcasting restrictions (effect on network contracts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations would prevent a station from granting an option to a network organization for any period of its broadcasting time; regulations barring exclusive contracts with affiliated stations had caused the networks ‘drastic damage.’ The network was prevented from furnishing its programs to any other station in the service area of its regular affiliate—even those programs which the regular affiliate did not carry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the concrete operational effects the Commission’s chain-broadcasting rules impose on networks and affiliates—limits on options and exclusivity and restrictions on program distribution within service areas; these effects were central to the networks’ legal challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional limitation on district courts re: injunctions when statute prescribes alternate remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court ‘Ruled unanimously … that a Federal District court lacks authority to enjoin enforcement of [the Emergency Price Control Act/related statute] because that law specifies [an alternate forum/procedure].’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a statute specifies an exclusive review route or special forum (e.g., Emergency Court of Appeals), district courts lack authority to enjoin enforcement of the statute; plaintiffs must use the statutory remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Census Bureau interpretation of unemployment estimates (short-duration and seasonal effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Census Bureau reported that ‘unemployment is now so low that a relatively large proportion of the persons included in the present estimate are workers “between jobs” for whom the duration of unemployment is short,’ and that increases in farm employment reflect seasonal/early hiring and return of temporarily employed workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistical unemployment estimates can be materially affected by short-duration transitions (people between jobs) and seasonal or early employment in agriculture; such context should accompany headline unemployment figures to avoid misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of appellate deference vs. policy questions
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is not for us to say that the ‘public interest’ will be furthered or retarded by the chain broadcasting regulations … such questions shall be passed on to Congress for the grant of legislative authority, and to the commission for its exercise.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will refrain from substituting judicial policy judgments for legislative or agency determinations about what serves the public interest; deference is appropriate where statutory standards and evidentiary findings exist.
